analysis.one_liner: Requires large social media platforms to share data with independent researchers and disclose ads, algorithms, and moderation.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced on December 21, 2022 with two Democrats and two Republicans behind it, was referred to the Senate HELP committee and died there 13 days later with no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force large social media platforms — those with 50 million or more U.S. monthly users — to hand data to vetted university and nonprofit researchers studying how the platforms affect society, through a joint program run by the National Science Foundation and the FTC. It would also require public, searchable libraries of ads (including who paid and how they were targeted), of widely spread content and major public accounts, and of statistics on content moderation and how recommendation algorithms work. To give the mandate teeth, it would strip platforms of their Section 230 legal immunity for claims caused by their refusal to comply.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary users of social media, who would get real visibility into who is paying to target them, how algorithms amplify or suppress content, and what platforms are removing. Academic researchers at U.S. universities and nonprofits would gain legally protected access to platform data they currently can only get at the platforms' discretion, and a safe harbor so scraping or running research accounts can't get them sued.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Social media users and independent researchers

how_it_helps.text: Creates an NSF-FTC research program that platforms must provide data to for approved, public-interest research projects, with the FTC setting privacy and cybersecurity safeguards and excluding direct messages, biometric data, and precise location from what can be shared.
Requires public, searchable repositories of advertising — the ad content, who paid for it, when it ran, how it was targeted, and whether the platform's algorithms amplified or restricted it.

Requires public disclosure of highly disseminated content and content from major public accounts, including metrics on how algorithms amplified or restricted it, plus statistics on content moderation, violating content prevalence, and how recommendation and ranking algorithms work.

Gives journalists and researchers a legal safe harbor to collect public platform data, use browser extensions with user consent, and run research accounts, so platforms cannot sue or shut down independent investigations.

Amends Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act so a platform found in final order to have refused a lawful data request loses its legal immunity for harms that refusal directly caused — the enforcement lever the rest of the bill otherwise lacks.

analysis.who_pays: Large platforms bear the compliance costs of building data pipelines, ad and content repositories, and algorithm reporting, and face public exposure of practices that currently stay behind closed doors. Taxpayers fund the NSF and FTC to run and enforce the program, which the bill authorizes open-ended appropriations for. Users carry a residual privacy risk if safeguards fail.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large social media platforms and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Moving large volumes of user data to outside researchers creates real leak and re-identification risks; the bill acknowledges this by requiring FTC-approved safeguards, encryption, de-identification, and deletion requirements, but no safeguard eliminates the risk.

The FTC would review researchers' findings before publication to screen out personal information and trade secrets, and the agencies' decisions on which projects are approved cannot be challenged in court — a structure that gives the government leverage over what research gets out, even though the bill bars denial based on a researcher's politics.
Platforms get a safe harbor from any lawsuit arising from the data releases to researchers, so a user harmed by a data leak under an approved project could not sue the platform for that release.

The research pathway is slow and narrow: only U.S. university and 501(c) nonprofit researchers qualify, projects need institutional review board approval, and platforms get the right to comment on and appeal any approval — which could drag projects out for months or years.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency gains are real: today platforms decide unilaterally what outsiders may learn about ads, amplification, and moderation, and researchers depend on their goodwill. The bill's genuine weaknesses are the privacy exposure of mass data sharing and the FTC's prepublication review, which cuts both ways on press freedom. Its enforcement teeth are also modest — the Section 230 penalty only applies after a final order of noncompliance, and platforms have appeal rights at every step. On balance a serious accountability bill, but one whose strongest provisions would likely have been contested heavily in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on December 21, 2022 and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never took it up before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Chris Coons introduced the bill on December 21, 2022 — thirteen days before the 117th Congress expired — with a bipartisan group: Democrats Coons and Amy Klobuchar and Republicans Rob Portman and Bill Cassidy.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day; that is the last action in the record.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever followed, and the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large social media platforms are better off: they never had to open their data, ad targeting, or moderation practices to outside researchers or the public, and kept their Section 230 immunity intact.

for.name: Sen. Chris Coons
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 21, 2022, with bipartisan cosponsors, in the final days of the 117th Congress.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Patty Murray, D-WA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on December 21, 2022 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was evenly bipartisan — two Democrats (Coons, Klobuchar) and two Republicans (Portman, Cassidy) — but no hearing or vote ever occurred, so there is no record of how the full Senate or any party bloc would have divided.

industries.industry: Large social media platforms (50M+ U.S. users)
industries.note: The bill would have required platforms like Facebook, YouTube, and TikTok to share user data with approved researchers, publish ad and content repositories, and report on their algorithms and moderation — and would have pierced their Section 230 immunity for refusing. Their business depends on controlling that information, which is why this bill sat in committee.

University and nonprofit researchers would gain a legal right to platform data for approved public-interest projects, plus a safe harbor for scraping and research accounts that they currently lack. The bill's prepublication review and safeguards would constrain how they use it.

Advertisers would have to disclose who paid for ads, how they were targeted, and which groups were excluded — ending opaque political and commercial targeting. The same disclosure also gives advertisers a public tool for accountability.
